title: Rio Tinto Pledges $250 Million to Confront the Toxic Legacy of Bougainville's Panguna Mine
summary: Rio Tinto will contribute $250 million to a fund addressing the environmental and human rights damage left by the former Panguna copper and gold mine in Bougainville, more than 35 years after the mine closed amid conflict — a landmark corporate accountability deal that still leaves the full clean-up bill unpaid.
content:
Rio Tinto will contribute $250 million over the coming years to a fund aimed at addressing the environmental and human rights damage left by the former Panguna copper and gold mine in Papua New Guinea's Bougainville region, the mining giant announced on Monday, November 16. The fund will be established jointly with the Autonomous Bougainville Government (ABG) and Bougainville Copper Limited (BCL), the ASX-listed operator of the mine, following consultations with community leaders, the company said in a statement, according to [Reuters](https://wncy.com/2026/11/16/rio-tinto-to-contribute-250-million-to-fund-addressing-bougainville-mine-legacy-impacts/).

The money will be used to initiate practical responses along the river and delta areas affected by decades of mining waste, as well as social programmes for communities across all impacted areas. Projects already under way in the region include the removal of hazardous materials at the former Loloho port, bridge construction, and a multi-year water and sanitation programme. Specific remedy plans have yet to be released, though Rio Tinto said all programmes will abide by the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.

The announcement closes a chapter that has haunted Bougainville for more than three decades. Panguna, once one of the largest copper mines in the world, operated from 1972 until 1989, when it was forced to shut amid an armed uprising rooted in anger over environmental destruction and the distribution of mining profits. The closure helped trigger a decade-long conflict that left thousands of people dead and the island's economy in ruins. Rio Tinto was formerly the majority shareholder in BCL, the mine's operator, before divesting its 53.8 percent stake in 2016 — a sale that, at the time, left affected communities with no corporate backer to turn to for remediation.

What changed the equation was an independent investigation. The Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment (PMLIA), published in December 2024 after a human rights complaint brought on behalf of local communities by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, found that the abandoned mine still posed several life-threatening risks, including unstable buildings and mine-related flooding. Tailings dumped into the Jaba and Kawerong river systems during the mine's operating years continue to choke waterways and threaten villages downstream, the assessment found. Rio Tinto, BCL and the ABG then set up a roundtable to address the findings, and it was from that process that the decision to establish the fund emerged.

The $250 million commitment — equivalent to roughly 1.1 billion Papua New Guinean kina — is substantial, but experts familiar with major mine rehabilitation projects caution that it will not cover the full cost of restoring the site. Instead, the fund is designed to pay for immediate, high-priority risk mitigation and community support while longer-term decisions are made. Its governance, delivery arrangements and detailed spending priorities have yet to be finalised, and the parties have stressed that the remediation fund and its activities will remain separate from any decision about the future of the mine and port. That decision, including whether Panguna might one day reopen, rests with the Autonomous Bougainville Government and the people of Bougainville, who voted overwhelmingly for independence in a 2019 referendum.

For corporate accountability campaigners, the deal is a landmark: a multinational agreeing to pay hundreds of millions of dollars for damage at a site it walked away from a decade ago, after years of pressure from the communities living with the consequences. It comes in the same week that the world's highest court delivered another accountability milestone, ruling that Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya, as reported in [Global Wire's coverage of the ICJ ruling](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/icj-to-rule-myanmar-rohingya-genocide-november-19-2026). Together, the two developments underline a shifting expectation that powerful institutions — whether states or corporations — can be made to answer for harms long after the fact.

Whether the Panguna fund delivers on its promise will depend on what happens next. Community leaders will be watching closely to see how quickly the money reaches the river valleys and villages that have waited 37 years for clean-up, and whether the governance of the fund gives them a genuine say in how it is spent. For now, the announcement marks the first time since the mine's closure that a concrete sum has been put on the table — and the first step, however belated, from assessing the damage toward repairing it. The Pacific region continues to face overlapping pressures from environmental damage and natural hazards, as seen in [this week's earthquake in eastern Indonesia](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/indonesia-earthquake-tual-magnitude-6-6-november-2026).
